finding: Act 125 of 2021 (the transmission infrastructure planning act, in effect Dec 17, 2021) gives the incumbent transmission company the right to build, own and operate a regionally cost-shared line approved by MISO when the line connects to that incumbent's facilities. It's commonly called a right-of-first-refusal (ROFR) law.
Lines longer than 5 miles at 345 kV or more need a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) from the Michigan PSC. A PSC certificate preempts local zoning.

Landowner opposition over eminent domain on ITC's ~50-mile Oneida–Sabine Lake line (Eaton to Livingston County). Two townships passed resolutions against the lines, and the PSC previously criticized METC's public engagement on earlier projects.
No ROFR law. MISO picked the developers for BECI (765 kV) and WISE (345 kV) by competitive bid in January 2026.

ROFR bills were introduced in 2021, 2023 and 2025 (SB 28 / AB 25) without becoming law. In 2026 incumbents asked FERC (Docket EL26-58) to pause competition, and a group of Wisconsin legislators filed comments opposing it.

New lines go through a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) at the Wisconsin PSC; the 2025 ROFR bill text refers to that application. Voltage and length thresholds weren't checked for this dashboard.

The Wisconsin PSC's draft Strategic Energy Assessment projects the state's peak rising from 14.2 GW to more than 20 GW by 2032, and ties more than 72% of 'that peak electricity load' to three data center developments. The article doesn't say whether that means the growth or the total; the growth is the likelier reading. The final report may change.
